Q183245.bio: George Frederic Watts was born in London and trained as a sculptor and painter. He painted portraits of the great and the good, as well as symbolic works on big themes like Hope and Love. In his later years he lived in the English village of Compton, where his gallery still stands. He died in 1904.

Q449519.bio: Richard Dadd was born in Chatham, England, and became a talented painter before he fell seriously ill in his twenties. He spent the rest of his life in hospitals, where he kept painting amazing, tiny, detailed fairy pictures. He lived in Bethlem and then Broadmoor Hospital. He died in 1886.

Q127171.bio: Jean-Honoré Fragonard was born in Grasse, in the south of France, and moved to Paris as a boy. He studied in Italy and became a star of the Rococo style, painting playful, romantic scenes for the nobility. After the French Revolution, his style fell out of fashion, and he spent his last years nearly forgotten in Paris. Today we again admire his speed and charm.

Q369263.bio: John Trumbull was born in Lebanon, Connecticut, and served as an officer in the American Revolution. Afterwards he studied painting in London with Benjamin West. He is best known for paintings of key events in the Revolution, such as the signing of the Declaration of Independence. He died in New York City in 1843.

Q561916.bio: Henry Raeburn was born in Stockbridge, near Edinburgh, Scotland, and became Scotland's best-known portrait painter. He painted writers, lawyers and clan chiefs with a lively, confident brush. He was knighted in 1822. He lived and worked in Edinburgh until his death in 1823.

Q241732.bio: Rosa Bonheur was born in Bordeaux, France, and grew up in Paris, where she studied animals at farms and markets. She became one of the most famous women artists of the 1800s, painting horses, cattle and sheep. She even got official permission to wear trousers in public so she could work. She died at her château in Thomery, near Paris, in 1899.

Q2272816.bio: Peder Balke was born on an island in Norway and became a painter who started out as a house painter. He traveled to Norway's far north and painted bold, simple pictures of the sea and mountains. His work went unnoticed in his lifetime but is admired today. He died in Christiania (Oslo) in 1887.

Q253446.bio: Anna Ancher was born in Skagen, Denmark, the daughter of an innkeeper. She became one of the greatest painters of the Skagen artists' colony, known for her use of light, and for her portraits and interiors. She married the painter Michael Ancher and lived her whole life in Skagen. She died there in 1935.

Q213973.bio: Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein was born in Haina, Germany, to a family of painters. He lived in Rome and Naples and became a friend of the poet Goethe. He painted portraits and scenes from mythology. He died in Eutin, Germany, in 1829.

Q4768.bio: Karl Bryullov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, into a family of artists. He lived for many years in Italy, where he painted his huge masterpiece 'The Last Day of Pompeii.' He returned to Russia as a celebrity and was admired by writers like Pushkin. He died in Italy in 1852.

Q134741.bio: Camille Pissarro was born on the island of St. Thomas in the Caribbean and moved to France as a teen. He was the oldest of the Impressionists and a father figure and teacher to many younger painters, including Cézanne. He painted farms, villages and city streets in France. He died in Paris in 1903.

Q158840.bio: James Ensor was born in Ostend, Belgium, and lived there nearly his whole life. He painted bizarre carnival masks, skeletons, and crowds in bright, shocking colors. His strange work was ahead of its time, and he became a hero for modern artists. He died in Ostend in 1949.

Q762949.bio: August Malmström was born in Sweden and became a painter of Nordic legends, fairy tales and landscapes. He studied in Stockholm and Düsseldorf. He later directed the Swedish National Museum's art school. He died in Stockholm in 1901.

Q310437.bio: Alexandre Cabanel was born in Montpellier, France, and became a star of the French Academy. He lived in Paris, where he taught at the École des Beaux-Arts. He painted classical and historical subjects, as well as portraits of the rich. Napoleon III admired him and bought his work.

Q351746.bio: Joaquín Sorolla was born in Valencia, Spain, and became known as the 'master of light' for his sparkling paintings of beaches and sunshine. He worked in Madrid and traveled to Paris and the United States, where he was very popular. His house in Madrid is now a museum. He died in Spain in 1923.

Q154349.bio: Odilon Redon was born in Bordeaux, France, and spent most of his life in Paris. He began with strange, dreamlike black-and-white drawings, then later painted flowers and myths in luminous color. His art was admired by Symbolists and later by the Surrealists. He died in Paris in 1916.

Q981441.bio: Wilhelm Bendz was born in Odense, Denmark, and studied in Copenhagen. He painted lively portraits of his artist friends and finely detailed scenes of daily life. He died of an illness at only 28 in Vicenza, Italy, in 1832.

Q184212.bio: Théodore Géricault was born in Rouen, France, and grew up in Paris, where he fell in love with horses and dramatic subjects. He studied wounded soldiers and even hospital patients so he could paint with truth. He rose to fame with 'The Raft of the Medusa' at 27. A passionate horse rider, he died in Paris at only 32, partly after riding accidents.

Q35548.bio: Paul Cézanne was born in Aix-en-Provence in southern France and lived there for much of his life, painting its hills, orchards, and the mountain Sainte-Victoire. He studied with the Impressionists in Paris, but then went his own way, building forms from blocks of color. He is often called the father of modern art, and both Picasso and Matisse praised him. He died in 1906 after catching a chill while painting outside.

Q146691.bio: Alphonse Mucha was born in Ivančice, in what is now the Czech Republic. He moved to Paris and became world-famous for his elegant Art Nouveau posters. Later in his life he returned to Prague and painted a huge series of paintings called the Slav Epic. He died in 1939.

Q4974655.bio: Sofie Ribbing was born in Sweden and became a painter and teacher who lived in Sweden, Denmark, and Norway. She studied in Copenhagen and was known for scenes of children and family life. She was one of the notable Scandinavian women painters of her era. She died in 1894.

Q40599.bio: Édouard Manet was born into a wealthy Parisian family and lived in Paris all his life. He painted modern city life — cafés, bars, and picnics — in a bold, flat style that scandalized critics. He never officially joined the Impressionists, but he inspired them, and they admired him as a leader. He died in 1883 at age 51.

Q5589.bio: Henri Matisse was born in northern France and began painting after an illness at age 20. He lived in Paris and then in Nice in the south, where he painted in bold, free colors. He was the leader of Fauvism, whose name means 'wild beasts', and later made colorful paper cut-outs. He died in Nice in 1954.

Q274298.bio: Edouard Louis Dubufe was born in Paris to a family of painters. He painted portraits and historical scenes for the French court and nobility. He was a successful society painter in the era of Napoleon III. He died in 1883.

Q483992.bio: William-Adolphe Bouguereau was born in La Rochelle, on France's Atlantic coast, and studied in Paris and Rome. He became the most celebrated painter of the French Academy, famous for smooth, glowing figures from myths and everyday life. He taught thousands of students. When Impressionism rose, he fell from fashion, but his technical skill is again widely admired.

Q23380.bio: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was born in Montauban, in southern France, and trained under David in Paris. He spent many years in Italy and in the end died in Paris. He believed in the power of clean, elegant outlines and was a master of portraits. He was also a fine violin player, and the phrase 'Ingres's violin' came to mean a talented hobby.

Q44007.bio: Paul Klee was born near Bern, Switzerland, to a musical family and was also a talented violinist. He taught at the Bauhaus, a famous art school in Germany, and later fled the Nazis to Switzerland. His playful, imaginative paintings use lines, colors and symbols as if they were music. He died in Switzerland in 1940.

Q45006.bio: Franz von Stuck was born in Bavaria, Germany, and became a celebrated painter and teacher in Munich. He was a founding member of the Munich Secession and painted mysterious and powerful symbolic pictures. Kandinsky and Klee were among his students. He lived in a grand villa in Munich, which is now a museum.

Q553258.bio: Francisco Pradilla y Ortiz was born in a small village in Aragón, Spain, and trained in Madrid and Rome. He became famous for large history paintings of kings and queens. He served as director of the Prado Museum. He died in Madrid in 1921.

Q156889.bio: Suzanne Valadon was born in a small town in France and moved to Paris as a girl. She worked as a circus performer and an artist's model for Renoir and Toulouse-Lautrec before teaching herself to paint. She became the first woman admitted to the French National Society of Fine Arts. She lived in Montmartre and died in Paris in 1938.

Q120993.bio: Amedeo Modigliani was born in Livorno, Italy, and moved to Paris in 1906. He painted and sculpted people with long necks, almond-shaped eyes, and elegant simplified faces. He was poor and ill throughout his short life and died in Paris at 35. Only after his death did his fame explode.

Q41513.bio: William Blake was born in London and lived there nearly his entire life. He was a poet, painter and printmaker who claimed to see angels and visions, and he created magical books mixing words and pictures. Few people understood him while he lived, and he was poor. Today he's honored as one of the greatest imaginations in British art and literature.

Q207447.bio: Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin was born in Paris, the son of a cabinet-maker. He became one of the greatest painters of still lifes and quiet scenes of everyday life in 1700s France. He worked slowly and carefully with a soft touch. He spent his entire life in Paris.

Q356644.bio: Albert Edelfelt was born in Finland to a Swedish family and studied in Antwerp and Paris. He painted portraits, scenes of Finnish life, and historical subjects. He was one of the most famous Finnish painters. He died in Finland in 1905.

Q175130.bio: Alfred Sisley was born in Paris to English parents and was one of the key Impressionist painters. He painted quiet landscapes along the Seine River and in small villages near Paris. He lived most of his life in France but remained a British citizen. He died in Moret-sur-Loing in 1899.

Q766362.bio: William Etty was born in York, England, and spent his life training to paint like the Old Masters. He is best known for his rich colors and glowing skin tones. He worked in London but retired to his hometown of York. He died there in 1849.

Q171344.bio: William Hogarth was born in London and became one of Britain's best-known painters and engravers. He made funny, sharp pictures about the follies of society, often in sets of prints that tell a story. He also championed the rights of artists. He died in London in 1764.

Q152797.bio: Umberto Boccioni was born in Reggio Calabria, Italy, and became the leader of Futurism, a movement that celebrated speed and machines. He worked in Milan and Rome, painting and making sculptures full of motion. He died at 33 after falling from a horse during military training in 1916.

Q118810.bio: Marie-Guillemine Benoist was born in Paris and studied with Vigée Le Brun and Jacques-Louis David. She was one of the leading women painters of her time and exhibited at the Paris Salon. Her 'Portrait of Madeleine' is one of the most celebrated works of the French Revolution era. She died in Paris in 1826.

Q61064.bio: Wassily Kandinsky was born in Moscow and trained as a lawyer before becoming a painter at age 30. He lived in Russia, Germany and later France. He is considered one of the first artists to paint truly abstract works, using color and shape like music. He died in Neuilly-sur-Seine, near Paris, in 1944.

Q363823.bio: Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg was born in southern Denmark and became the 'father of Danish painting.' He studied in Paris and Rome and taught many painters in Copenhagen. He painted portraits, ships, and clear, bright scenes of Rome. He died in Copenhagen in 1853.

Q964791.bio: Paul Émile Chabas was born in Nantes, France, and became a popular painter in Paris. He is best known for dreamy paintings of young people by lakes and meadows in soft light. His work was admired by the public in the early 1900s. He died in Paris in 1937.

Q41406.bio: Edvard Munch was born in Norway and grew up in Christiania (now Oslo), in a family troubled by illness and loss. He traveled in Europe, especially Germany and France, and used paint to express anxiety, love and loneliness. His most famous work, 'The Scream', is among the best-known images ever. He spent his last decades at his estate Ekely near Oslo and died in 1944.

Q271484.bio: Marguerite Gérard was born in Grasse, France, and moved to Paris as a teenager to train with her brother-in-law, Fragonard. She became a successful painter of elegant home scenes, often showing women reading, writing or playing music. She exhibited at the Salon and sold to the wealthy collectors of Europe. She died in Paris in 1837.

Q64633.bio: George Peter Alexander Healy was born in Boston and became a portrait painter who worked in Paris, Rome, Chicago and Washington. He painted American presidents and the kings and queens of Europe. He lived long in Europe before settling in Chicago. He died there in 1894.

Q457976.bio: Nikolai Ge was born in Voronezh, Russia, and studied in Saint Petersburg and Italy. He painted powerful scenes from history and religion with dramatic light and strong emotion. Later in life he lived on a farm in Ukraine. He died in 1894.

Q702272.bio: Johann Zoffany was born in Frankfurt, Germany, and moved to London. He painted 'conversation pieces' — groups of people in rooms and gardens — as well as theatrical scenes. He traveled to Italy and India, and became a favorite of the British royal family. He died in London in 1810.

Q37693.bio: Paul Gauguin was born in Paris and spent part of childhood in Peru. He worked as a stockbroker before turning to painting full-time. He lived in Brittany, in Arles with Van Gogh, and then in Tahiti and the Marquesas Islands in the South Pacific, seeking a simpler life. His flat, vivid colors influenced Picasso and Matisse.

Q922483.bio: William Orpen was born near Dublin, Ireland, and became a leading portrait painter in London. He served as an official war artist in World War I and painted the Paris Peace Conference. He died in London in 1931.

Q110228.bio: Vasily Surikov was born in Krasnoyarsk, in Siberia, and moved to Moscow and Saint Petersburg. He painted huge history scenes of Russia's past with crowds of vivid individuals. His paintings are among Russia's most loved. He died in Moscow in 1916.

Q7724.bio: August Strindberg was born in Stockholm, Sweden, and is best known as one of the world's greatest playwrights and novelists. He also painted dramatic, stormy landscapes in his later years, which were far ahead of their time. He lived in Sweden, Germany, France and Denmark. He died in Stockholm in 1912.

Q77132.bio: Albert Bierstadt was born in Germany and raised in Massachusetts. He traveled west with survey expeditions and painted vast landscapes of the Rocky Mountains and Yosemite. His work was admired by huge crowds in the East. He lived in New York and died there in 1902.

Q381248.bio: James Tissot was born in Nantes, France, and moved to London, where he painted fashionable scenes of Victorian life. Later he traveled to the Holy Land and made a famous series of illustrations of the Bible. He was a very successful artist. He died in France in 1902.

Q1190012.bio: Osman Hamdi Bey was born in Istanbul, in the Ottoman Empire, and studied painting in Paris. He was also an archaeologist and founded Istanbul's first modern art school and archaeological museum. His paintings show scenes of Ottoman life with great detail. He died in 1910 and is honored as a pioneer of Turkish art.

Q448189.bio: Jacek Malczewski was born in Radom, Poland, and became a leading Symbolist painter. He studied in Kraków and Paris and often painted himself in dreamlike scenes full of Polish folklore and history. He lived in Kraków, where he later taught. He died there in 1929.

Q958052.bio: Konstantin Savitsky was born in Taganrog, Russia, and studied at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg. He was a member of the Peredvizhniki, or 'Wanderers,' a group who took realistic art to ordinary people around Russia. He was known for paintings of people and animals. He died in 1905 in Penza.

Q192720.bio: Thomas Gainsborough was born in Sudbury, a small town in England, and moved to London as a teenager to study art. He became one of Britain's most fashionable portrait painters, working in Bath and London. He secretly preferred painting landscapes, and he loved music. His elegant, feathery brushstrokes made his sitters seem alive.

Q211763.bio: William Holman Hunt was born in London and, with Millais and Rossetti, founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848. He traveled to the Middle East to paint biblical scenes with realistic backgrounds. His most famous painting is 'The Light of the World'. He died in London in 1910.

Q204138.bio: Viktor Vasnetsov was born in a village in northern Russia, the son of a priest. He lived in Moscow, and became known for painting scenes from Russian folk tales and legends, with warriors, witches and firebirds. He also designed churches and theater sets. He died in Moscow in 1926.

Q313498.bio: Benjamin West was born near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and moved to Europe in his twenties. He settled in London, where he became the history painter to King George III and later President of the Royal Academy. He taught many American painters. He died in London in 1820.

Q328369.bio: Edwin Landseer was born in London and showed an extraordinary talent for drawing animals as a child. He became Queen Victoria's favorite animal painter, and he created the bronze lions at the base of Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square. He painted dogs, horses, and stags with great warmth. He died in London in 1873.

Q187506.bio: Honoré Daumier was born in Marseille, France, and grew up in Paris. He was famous for his satirical cartoons that poked fun at politicians, and he created thousands of prints. He also painted sympathetic pictures of working people. He lost his sight late in life and died in 1879.

Q123757.bio: Jean-Étienne Liotard was born in Geneva, Switzerland, and traveled across Europe and to Constantinople. He is best known for pastel portraits with a precise, glowing look. He worked for royals and nobles in Vienna, Paris and England. He died in Geneva in 1789.

Q83155.bio: Jacques-Louis David was born in Paris and became the greatest painter of the Neoclassical style, inspired by ancient Greece and Rome. He supported the French Revolution and later became Napoleon's official painter. After Napoleon fell, he was forced into exile and spent his last years in Brussels, Belgium. He taught many famous students and shaped French art for generations.

Q1763678.bio: Henry Holiday was born in London and was a painter, designer and stained-glass artist. He was influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites. He also illustrated Lewis Carroll's poem 'The Hunting of the Snark'. He died in London in 1927.

Q347139.bio: Jean-Baptiste Greuze was born in Tournus, France, and moved to Paris, where he became famous for sentimental paintings of family life and young girls with moral messages. He was admired by the philosopher Diderot. His popularity faded after the French Revolution. He died in Paris in 1805.

Q151803.bio: Piet Mondrian was born in the Netherlands and started out painting windmills and trees. He lived in Amsterdam, Paris, London and finally New York City. Over time he simplified his art into straight black lines and blocks of red, yellow and blue. He died in New York in 1944, and his style inspired architects and designers worldwide.

Q123071.bio: Arnold Böcklin was born in Basel, Switzerland, and spent long periods in Italy and Germany. He painted dreamy scenes full of myths, strange creatures and mysterious islands. He is best known for 'Isle of the Dead'. He died near Florence in 1901.

Q1528580.bio: Giuseppe Pellizza da Volpedo was born in Volpedo, in northern Italy, and lived there much of his life. He painted in the style of dots and fine brushstrokes of pointillism. His masterpiece 'The Fourth Estate' shows workers marching for their rights. He died in 1907 at age 39.

Q458671.bio: Giuseppe Castiglione was born in Milan, Italy, and became a Jesuit brother, traveling as a missionary to China. He took the name Lang Shining and served as a court painter for three Chinese emperors. He blended European realism with Chinese styles. He died in Beijing in 1766.

Q41402.bio: Gilbert Stuart was born in Rhode Island and became America's best-known portrait painter. He painted George Washington and other leaders of the young United States. He lived for years in London and Dublin before returning to the U.S. He died in Boston in 1828.

Q366212.bio: Frederic Edwin Church was born in Hartford, Connecticut, and studied with Thomas Cole. He traveled to South America, the Arctic and the Middle East, painting giant landscapes full of wonder. He became one of the most famous artists in the United States. He built a Persian-style mansion called Olana on the Hudson River.

Q1470796.bio: Frederick Sandys was born in Norwich, England, and became a painter and illustrator associated with the Pre-Raphaelites. He was famous for detailed portraits of beautiful women. He lived in London, and he died there in 1904.

Q160252.bio: Frederic Leighton was born in Scarborough, England, and traveled across Europe as a child, speaking several languages. He became a leading Victorian painter of classical subjects and was President of the Royal Academy. He was the first British artist to be made a baron. His house in London is now a museum.

Q295144.bio: Gustave Caillebotte was born into a wealthy Paris family and trained as a lawyer and engineer before painting. He was an Impressionist, but his pictures often show unusual high or low perspectives of the modern city. He generously used his money to support his friends, buying their paintings. He lived near Paris and died in Gennevilliers at 45.

Q381728.bio: George Stubbs was born in Liverpool, England, and taught himself to paint. He studied horse anatomy by dissecting horses and published a famous book about it. He became Britain's finest painter of horses and other animals. He died in London in 1806.

Q182664.bio: Giovanni Antonio Canal, known as Canaletto, was born in Venice and painted its canals, palaces, and festivals with great precision. His views were popular with wealthy British visitors on their tours of Italy, and he lived in London for several years. His paintings are still the way many people picture Venice. He died in Venice in 1768.

Q148458.bio: Jean-François Millet was born into a farming family in Gruchy, on the coast of Normandy, France. He moved to the village of Barbizon near Paris, where he painted peasants at work in the fields. He treated farm laborers with dignity at a time when few artists did. His paintings moved Van Gogh and many others.

Q1795226.bio: Walenty Wańkowicz was born in a village in what is now Belarus and studied in Vilnius. He became a Polish painter famous for portraits of poets, including Adam Mickiewicz. He lived in Saint Petersburg and in Paris. He died in Paris in 1842.

Q380494.bio: Charles Demuth was born in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and studied art in Philadelphia and Paris. He was a leading American modernist known for crisp, precise paintings of buildings and factories. He lived with diabetes for most of his adult life. He died in Lancaster in 1935.

Q365068.bio: P. S. Krøyer was born in Stavanger, Norway, and grew up in Copenhagen, Denmark. He was the central figure of the Skagen Painters, an artist colony in northern Denmark. His paintings capture the beautiful blue light of summer evenings by the sea. He died in Skagen in 1909.

Q3048418.bio: Edvard Isto was born in northern Finland and became a painter who studied in Helsinki and Paris. He is best known for 'The Attack,' which became a symbol of Finnish resistance. He died in Helsinki in 1905, at the age of 40.

Q364226.bio: Kuzma Petrov-Vodkin was born in a small town on the Volga River in Russia, and trained in Moscow, Saint Petersburg, and Paris. He used Russian icon painting as inspiration for his bold, simple style. He later taught in Saint Petersburg (then Leningrad). He died there in 1939.

Q583015.bio: Jacques Amans was born in Maastricht, in the Netherlands, and worked as a portrait painter in France and the United States. He lived in New Orleans for several years in the 1830s and painted many local families. He returned to Paris, where he died in 1888.

Q240526.bio: Lawrence Alma-Tadema was born in a village in the Netherlands and settled in London, England, in 1870. He became famous for sunny paintings of ancient Rome and Greece, filled with marble, flowers, and sea views. He was knighted and extremely popular during his lifetime. He died in Wiesbaden, Germany, in 1912.

Q22583666.bio: Carl Kahler was born in Linz, Austria, and emigrated to the United States, where he worked in San Francisco. He painted landscapes, horses and animals. His giant painting of 42 cats made him famous, and he took three years to complete it. He died in 1906.

Q315102.bio: Alexander Roslin was born in Malmö, Sweden, and became a leading portrait painter at the French court. He lived in Paris, where he painted queens, kings and the leading minds of the day. His specialty was the shimmer of silks and satins. He died in Paris in 1793.

Q318393.bio: Vasily Polenov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, and became a leading landscape painter and teacher. He traveled in Europe and the Middle East. He built an estate on the Oka River that is now a museum. He died in 1927.

Q322582.bio: Paul Delaroche was born in Paris and became one of France's most popular painters of dramatic history scenes. He worked and taught in Paris, where he trained many future artists. His paintings often show famous tragedies, such as the death of royalty. He died in Paris in 1856.

Q217128.bio: Valentin Serov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, to a musical family. He studied under Repin and became Russia's most sought-after portrait painter, painting writers, musicians, and even the tsar. He lived mostly in Moscow. His portraits are admired for being fresh, sunny and natural.

Q212754.bio: John William Waterhouse was born in Rome to English parents and later lived in London. He painted women from myths and legends — such as the Lady of Shalott and sirens — in lush, colorful detail. He admired the Pre-Raphaelites, who came before him. He died in London in 1917.

Q155626.bio: John Singer Sargent was born in Florence, Italy, to American parents and grew up traveling around Europe. He trained in Paris, then worked mostly in London, becoming the most sought-after portrait painter of his day. He painted with dazzling, confident brushwork and also made lovely watercolors on trips to Venice and the Alps. During World War I he painted soldiers at the front. He died in London in 1925.

Q235903.bio: Evelyn De Morgan was born in London and studied at the Slade School of Art. She was a Pre-Raphaelite painter who painted glowing allegories about peace, war and the spirit. She lived in London and Florence and was also a pacifist and a supporter of women's rights. She died in 1919.

Q310715.bio: Henri Fantin-Latour was born in Grenoble, France, and spent most of his life in Paris. He was a friend of Manet and the Impressionists, though his own style was more traditional. He painted lovely flowers and group portraits of artists and musicians. He died in 1904.

Q937096.bio: John Martin was born in Northumberland, England, and made huge, dramatic paintings of disasters from the Bible and history. His work was hugely popular in London in the 1820s and 1830s, as thrilling as a movie. He also designed engineering schemes for his city. He died on the Isle of Man in 1854.

Q539474.bio: Constantin Hansen was born in Rome to Danish parents and grew up in Copenhagen. He was a leading painter of the Danish Golden Age and painted portraits, historical scenes and murals. He also visited Italy. He died near Copenhagen in 1880.

Q39931.bio: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was born in Limoges, France, and started his working life painting designs on porcelain. In Paris he became a founding Impressionist, famous for glowing scenes of friends, dancing, and sunshine. Later in life he lived in the warm south of France, and he kept painting even when arthritis twisted his hands, with a brush strapped to his fingers. He left thousands of cheerful paintings.

Q548914.bio: Philipp Veit was born in Berlin and became a painter in the Nazarene movement, a group who admired the art of medieval and Renaissance Germany and Italy. He lived in Rome, Frankfurt and Mainz. He was also a museum director. He died in Mainz in 1877.

Q82445.bio: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was born into a noble family in Albi, France, but broken bones in childhood stunted his growth. He moved to Montmartre in Paris and painted the dancers, singers and cabaret stars of the Moulin Rouge. His bold posters helped invent modern advertising art. He died at 36, at his mother's château in southwestern France.

Q159606.bio: John Everett Millais was born in Southampton, England, and was a child prodigy who entered the Royal Academy at 11. He co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a group that painted with bright color and fine detail. Later he became a famous society painter and was made a baronet, the first artist to receive that honor. He ended his life as President of the Royal Academy in London.

Q223725.bio: Francesco Hayez was born in Venice, Italy, and later became the leading painter in Milan. He painted history scenes that stirred Italian pride during the fight for unification of Italy. He also made fine portraits. He lived to be 91, long enough to see Italy become one country.

Q142420.bio: Edmund Blair Leighton was born in London and became famous for painting romantic scenes from the Middle Ages and the Regency period. He studied at the Royal Academy and lived in London. His paintings of knights and ladies are widely reproduced. He died in 1922.

Q44054.bio: Franz Marc was born in Munich, Germany, and loved painting animals as a symbol of purity. He co-founded the Blue Rider group with Wassily Kandinsky, and he used bold colors like blue and yellow to express feelings. He lived in Bavaria. He died in World War I in 1916 at age 36.

Q164961.bio: Adolph von Menzel was born in Breslau (now Wrocław, Poland) and lived most of his life in Berlin. He was Germany's greatest realist painter and an amazing draftsman. He painted history scenes, factories and daily life. He was a very short man who worked until his death in 1905.

Q193064.bio: Ivan Shishkin was born in the town of Yelabuga, in Russia, and became the great poet of the Russian forest. He lived in Saint Petersburg and traveled into the countryside to sketch trees in incredible detail. His pine and birch forests are among the most loved Russian paintings. He worked up until the day he died at his easel in 1898.

Q159297.bio: John Constable was born in East Bergholt, in the English county of Suffolk, where his father owned mills. He painted the farms, rivers, and clouds of the countryside he grew up in, often outdoors, which was unusual at the time. He lived in London for much of his adult life. He was more admired in France than at home, and his work inspired the Barbizon painters and Impressionists.

Q547055.bio: Carl Bloch was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, and became one of the country's most beloved painters of history and religious scenes. He spent years studying in Italy. His pictures of Bible stories are reproduced all over the world. He died in Copenhagen in 1890.

Q380052.bio: Mariano Fortuny Marsal was born in Reus, Spain, and became one of the best-known Spanish painters of the 1800s. He traveled to Morocco and painted bright, detailed scenes. He lived in Rome and Madrid, and died young in Rome in 1874, at age 36.

Q1390711.bio: Kolë Idromeno was born in Shkodër, Albania, and became a painter, architect and sculptor. He studied in Italy and is regarded as a pioneer of modern Albanian art. He designed buildings in his hometown. He died in Shkodër in 1939.

Q34661.bio: Gustav Klimt was born near Vienna, Austria, the son of a gold engraver, which may be why gold glitters in so many of his paintings. He lived his entire life in and around Vienna and co-founded the Vienna Secession, a group of artists who broke from tradition. He painted beautiful portraits, murals, and landscapes. He died in 1918 at age 55 after a stroke.

Q44032.bio: Egon Schiele was born in Tulln, Austria, and studied art in Vienna as a teenager. He was inspired by Gustav Klimt and developed a raw, angular and expressive drawing style. He lived in Vienna and in smaller Austrian towns. He died of the Spanish flu in 1918 at just 28, three days after his wife.

Q170068.bio: Akseli Gallen-Kallela was born in Pori, Finland, and became the country's most famous painter. He painted scenes from the Kalevala, Finland's national epic, and studied in Paris. He lived in Finland and traveled to Africa and the United States. He died in Stockholm in 1931.

Q28867.bio: Juan Luna was born in the Philippines and studied art in Manila, Madrid and Rome. His enormous painting 'Spoliarium' won a gold medal in Madrid in 1884, and made him a hero to Filipinos. He lived in Spain and France and supported Philippine independence. He died in Hong Kong in 1899.

Q172911.bio: Ilya Repin was born in a small town in Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire. He trained in Saint Petersburg and traveled to Paris before becoming Russia's most celebrated realist painter. He lived much of his later life in a country house near the Finnish border, now a museum. His huge paintings of people, history, and ordinary life made him a national treasure.

Q216406.bio: Edward Burne-Jones was born in Birmingham, England, and moved to London to become an artist. He was part of the second wave of Pre-Raphaelites and also designed stained glass and tapestries with William Morris. His dreamy paintings were inspired by medieval legends and myths. He was made a baronet and died in London in 1898.

Q169311.bio: Johann Friedrich Overbeck was born in Lübeck, Germany, and moved to Rome, where he led the Nazarenes, a group of artists inspired by medieval and early Renaissance painting. He lived in a former monastery with his friends. He stayed in Rome the rest of his life and died there in 1869.

Q452321.bio: Emanuel Leutze was born in Schwäbisch Gmünd, Germany, and moved to the United States as a child. He later studied in Düsseldorf, Germany, and lived there for years while painting American history scenes. He returned to the U.S. in 1859 and worked in Washington, D.C. His painting of Washington crossing the Delaware became a national icon.

Q334001.bio: Thomas Cole was born in England and moved to the United States as a teenager, settling near the Hudson River in New York. He founded the Hudson River School, a group of artists who painted America's wild landscapes. His paintings often carried messages about nature and civilization. He died in Catskill, New York, in 1848.

Q468772.bio: Anne Vallayer-Coster was born in Paris and became famous for lifelike still-life paintings of flowers, fruit and musical instruments. She was admitted to the French Royal Academy at 26 and also painted portraits. She worked for Queen Marie Antoinette. She died in Paris in 1818.

Q918605.bio: Herbert James Draper was born in London and studied at the Royal Academy. He painted scenes from Greek and Roman myth with glowing color and graceful figures. His 'The Lament for Icarus' is his best-known work. He died in London in 1920.

Q5432.bio: Francisco Goya was born in a small village in Spain and became the court painter to the Spanish kings in Madrid. After an illness left him deaf in his forties, his art grew darker and more personal. He witnessed war and cruelty and made powerful pictures about it. He spent his last years in Bordeaux, France, and is seen as a bridge between old masters and modern art.

Q2159499.bio: Roberto Ferruzzi was born in what is now Croatia and lived in Italy, mostly in Venice and nearby. He painted people and village scenes. His painting 'Madonnina' made him a celebrity when it won a prize in 1897. He died in 1934.

Q104884.bio: Caspar David Friedrich was born in the Baltic port of Greifswald, Germany, and later settled in Dresden. He painted quiet, mysterious landscapes of mountains, fog, ruins, and seashores, often with a tiny figure seen from behind. He believed nature was a way of feeling something divine. He became a hero of German Romanticism, though he was nearly forgotten for decades before being rediscovered.

Q453972.bio: John Collier was born in London and studied art in London, Paris and Munich. He painted portraits and scenes from history and legend, often with strong feelings. He also wrote about art and science. He died in London in 1934.

Q134150.bio: Marie Spartali Stillman was born in London to a Greek family and became one of the few women to be a respected Pre-Raphaelite painter. She studied with Ford Madox Brown. She modeled for other artists, too. She lived in London and Italy and died in 1927.

Q2199553.bio: Laurits Andersen Ring was born in a village in Denmark and became a leading Danish painter. He is known for quiet, thoughtful scenes of country life and portraits of his family. He lived and worked in the Danish countryside. He died in 1933.

Q34618.bio: Gustave Courbet was born in Ornans, in eastern France, and moved to Paris to become an artist. He led the Realism movement, insisting on painting real people and real life instead of myths. He was outspoken and got into political trouble, and he fled to Switzerland in the end. He died there in 1877.

Q159758.bio: J. M. W. Turner was born in London, the son of a barber, and became a student at the Royal Academy at just 14. He traveled across Britain and Europe, painting storms, ships, and sunsets in swirling light and color. He called the sky his subject, and his late paintings are almost abstract. He left thousands of works to the British nation when he died in London in 1851.

Q215100.bio: Mikhail Vrubel was born in Omsk, Siberia, and studied in Saint Petersburg. He lived in Russia and Ukraine, creating glittering, mosaic-like paintings and designs for theaters. He is best known for paintings of the Demon, a moody figure from a Russian poem. He lost his sight in later life and died in Saint Petersburg in 1910.

Q181568.bio: Ivan Aivazovsky was born in Feodosia, a port town on the Crimean coast of the Black Sea. He became one of the greatest painters of the sea, producing about 6,000 works in his career. He traveled widely in Europe and served as a Russian navy painter. He lived most of his life in Feodosia, where he built a studio and art gallery for his hometown.

Q911575.bio: Paul Baudry was born in La Roche-sur-Yon, France, and trained in Paris and Rome. He painted elegant portraits and murals, including the ceiling of the Paris Opera foyer. His work was admired by the Emperor Napoleon III. He died in Paris in 1886.

Q180932.bio: François Boucher was born in Paris and became the favorite painter of Madame de Pompadour, the French king's companion. He lived in Paris and was the leading figure in the Rococo style, with its pastel colors and playful, romantic scenes. He painted, designed tapestries and decorated palaces. He died in Paris in 1770.

Q2065760.bio: Władysław Podkowiński was born in Warsaw, Poland, and was a leading Impressionist and Symbolist painter. He studied in Warsaw and Paris, and he is remembered for the shocking 'Frenzy of Exultations.' He died young, at 29, in 1895.

Q720035.bio: Nicolaas Pieneman was born in Amersfoort, in the Netherlands, and became a portrait and history painter in Amsterdam. He painted royalty, battle scenes and a famous picture of the arrest of the Javanese prince Diponegoro. He died in Amsterdam in 1860.

Q105320.bio: Berthe Morisot was born in Bourges, France, and studied painting with Corot. She exhibited in the first Impressionist show in 1874 and was one of the movement's leading figures. She married Eugène Manet, the brother of Édouard Manet, and lived in Paris. She painted women, children and gardens with a light, fresh touch.

Q3370554.bio: Paul Balze was born in Rome to French parents and became a painter and student of Ingres. He lived and worked mostly in Paris, and was known for careful, classical work. He also copied works of the old masters. He died in Paris in 1884.

Q186748.bio: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was born in London to an Italian family of poets and scholars. He co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and painted dreamy, romantic women. He was also a poet, and often paired paintings with verses. He lived in London and died in 1882.

Q265665.bio: Pierre Auguste Cot was born in the south of France and became a popular painter in Paris. He studied with Bouguereau and painted romantic and mythological subjects. His paintings were very popular in America. He died in 1883.

Q691796.bio: Abanindranath Tagore was born in Kolkata (Calcutta), India, into a famous family that included the poet Rabindranath Tagore. He founded the Bengal School of art, which revived Indian painting styles. His work inspired the movement for India's independence. He died in Kolkata in 1951.

Q207298.bio: Frédéric Bazille was born into a wealthy family in Montpellier, France, and moved to Paris to paint. He was a close friend of Monet and Renoir and shared a studio with them. He painted sunny outdoor scenes and portraits. He was killed in the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 when he was only 28.

Q296.bio: Claude Monet was born in Paris but grew up on the coast of Normandy, where he learned to paint outdoors. He was a leader of Impressionism, and he lived in places like Argenteuil and, for his last 43 years, Giverny, where he built a famous garden with a pond of water lilies. He painted the same scenes again and again at different times of day to capture changing light. He kept painting until he was 86, even as his eyesight faded.

Q316016.bio: John Singleton Copley was born in Boston and became America's finest portrait painter before the Revolution. He painted merchants and patriots, like Paul Revere. In 1774 he moved to England as war loomed, and spent the rest of his life in London. He died there in 1815.

Q5582.bio: Vincent van Gogh was born in a small village in the Netherlands and worked as a teacher and art dealer before becoming a painter at age 27. He lived in the Netherlands, Belgium, Paris, and finally the sunny south of France, where his colors grew brighter and bolder. He painted more than 800 paintings in about a decade, yet sold almost none while alive. After his death at 37, his brother's family helped make him one of the most loved artists in history.

Q173223.bio: Mary Cassatt was born near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and moved to Paris as a young woman. She was the only American to join the French Impressionists, and she specialized in tender pictures of mothers and children. She lived in France most of her life, and she also encouraged American collectors to buy Impressionist art. She died at her country home in France in 1926.

Q46373.bio: Edgar Degas was born in Paris to a well-to-do family and lived there almost all his life. He's linked to the Impressionists, but preferred to work indoors, painting ballet dancers, racehorses, and women at their daily routines. He loved to catch unusual angles, as if a camera had snapped the scene. In old age his eyesight failed and he turned to sculpture.

Q718795.bio: Vincenzo Camuccini was born in Rome and became one of Italy's leading Neoclassical painters. He painted big history scenes and was in charge of the Vatican's paintings. He was also a collector. He died in Rome in 1844.

Q979541.bio: Martinus Rørbye was born in Drammen, Norway, and moved to Denmark as a child. He was a leading painter of the Danish Golden Age and traveled to Italy, Greece, and Turkey. He painted precise scenes of streets, interiors and windows. He died in Copenhagen in 1848.

Q958927.bio: Aleksander Gierymski was born in Warsaw, Poland, and studied in Germany and Italy. He painted moonlit city scenes, with great honesty about everyday life. He lived in Warsaw and later in Rome, where he spent his last years. He died in 1901.

Q122382.bio: Henry Fuseli was born in Zurich, Switzerland, and moved to England as a young man. He became a professor at the Royal Academy in London. He loved stories of ghosts, witches, and nightmares and painted them with dramatic, wild imagination. His artwork influenced the Romantic movement and later the Surrealists.

Q3290532.bio: John Steuart Curry was born on a farm in Kansas and became one of the main painters of the Regionalist movement, which celebrated the American Midwest. He painted farm life, storms and big moments from history. He also painted murals for the Kansas State Capitol. He died in Wisconsin in 1946.

Q212499.bio: Jean-Léon Gérôme was born in Vesoul, France, and became one of the most successful painters and teachers in Paris. He traveled to Egypt and the Middle East and painted lively scenes from ancient and modern life. He was also a sculptor. His students came from around the world.

Q433434.bio: Anne-Louis Girodet was born in Montargis, France, and studied under Jacques-Louis David. He became a leader of French Romanticism with dreamy, mysterious paintings. He lived in Rome and Paris. He died in Paris in 1824.

Q164735.bio: Johan Christian Dahl was born in Bergen, Norway, and became known as the father of Norwegian landscape painting. He lived most of his life in Dresden, Germany, where he was a friend of Caspar David Friedrich. He painted clouds, mountains and fjords with great realism. He died in Dresden in 1857.

Q34013.bio: Georges Seurat was born in Paris and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts. He invented pointillism, painting with tiny dots of pure color that blend in the viewer's eye. He worked slowly and carefully in his studio, making many sketches before big paintings. He died suddenly at only 31, leaving behind just a handful of masterpieces.

Q216999.bio: Antoine-Jean Gros was born in Paris and was a student of Jacques-Louis David. He became Napoleon's war painter, traveling with the army to capture battles and heroic scenes. His lively, dramatic art influenced the Romantic painters. He died in 1835 near Paris.

Q1293506.bio: Edward Savage was born in Massachusetts and was an American painter and engraver. He painted George Washington from life and made popular prints of his work. He lived in Philadelphia, New York and Boston. He died in 1817.

Q130777.bio: Kazimir Malevich was born near Kyiv, in what is now Ukraine, to a family of Polish origin. He lived in Moscow and Saint Petersburg and founded Suprematism, an art of pure shapes and colors. He also taught, wrote, and designed. After the Russian government turned against modern art, he was forced to return to simple realist styles before his death in 1935.

Q214062.bio: Joseph Wright of Derby was born in Derby, England, and spent nearly his whole life there. He was famous for painting scenes lit by a single candle or lamp, often showing scientific experiments. His friends included inventors and scientists of the Industrial Revolution. He's often called the first painter to capture the spirit of the Age of Science.

Q7422343.bio: Sarah Goodridge was born in Templeton, Massachusetts, and taught herself to paint miniature portraits. She worked in Boston, where she was a well-known painter of tiny portraits on ivory. She painted the great statesmen of her day, including Daniel Webster and Gilbert Stuart. She never married and ran her own successful art business.

Q2833597.bio: Alexandre Desgoffe was born in Paris and trained as a landscape painter under Ingres's circle. He spent his career in Paris, where he became known for classical landscapes in the Italian style. He exhibited for decades and received several honors. He died in Paris in 1882.

Q229272.bio: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner was born in Aschaffenburg, Germany, and trained as an architect before he became a founder of the group Die Brücke ('The Bridge'). He lived in Dresden and Berlin and later in the Swiss Alps near Davos. His jagged, colorful paintings made him a star of German Expressionism. He died in Switzerland in 1938.

Q203643.bio: James McNeill Whistler was born in Lowell, Massachusetts, in the United States, and spent his childhood partly in Russia. He moved to Europe as a young man and lived in Paris and London, where he became one of the most famous (and sharp-tongued) artists in the world. He titled paintings like pieces of music, such as 'Nocturne' and 'Arrangement.' He died in London in 1903.

Q318427.bio: Mikhail Nesterov was born in Ufa, Russia, and became a leading painter of religious and spiritual scenes. He painted frescoes in churches and created poetic pictures of saints in Russian landscapes. He lived through the Russian Revolution and continued painting in Moscow. He died there in 1942.

Q123098.bio: Angelica Kauffman was born in Chur, Switzerland, and was a child prodigy who traveled across Europe as a teen artist. She lived in Italy and London, where she became a founding member of the Royal Academy of Arts. She painted portraits and scenes from myth and history. She died in Rome in 1807.

Q353008.bio: Alexei Savrasov was born in Moscow and taught at the Moscow School of Painting. His painting 'The Rooks Have Returned' is often seen as the start of the Russian landscape tradition. He painted ordinary rural scenes with deep feeling. He died in Moscow in 1897.

Q189117.bio: Jan Matejko was born in Kraków, Poland, and became the nation's great painter of history. He made huge canvases of Poland's glories and heartbreaks, at a time when Poland was no longer an independent country. He lived most of his life in Kraków, where he later directed the School of Fine Arts. He's a national hero for keeping Polish memory alive.

Q6394591.bio: Vasily Pukirev was born in the Tula region of Russia and became a painter and teacher in Moscow. His most famous painting, 'The Unequal Marriage,' criticized forced marriages. It was a sensation, and he later taught at the Moscow School of Painting. He died in 1890.

Q263080.bio: Hugo Simberg was born in Hamina, Finland, and studied art in Helsinki and Paris. He lived mainly in Finland and painted strange, gentle scenes full of angels, devils, and skeletons, often with a wink of humor. His work blends Finnish folk tales with Symbolism. He died in 1917 at age 43.

Q434575.bio: Arthur Hughes was born in London and was an English painter linked to the Pre-Raphaelites. He is best known for glowing, romantic scenes of young lovers and medieval stories. He worked in London and in the countryside, and he also illustrated children's books. He died in 1915.

Q365544.bio: Adolph Tidemand was born in Mandal, Norway, and trained in Copenhagen and Düsseldorf. He lived much of his life in Germany and Norway, painting scenes of Norwegian farmers and folk traditions. He helped create the image of Norwegian national identity in the 1800s. He died in Christiania in 1876.

Q381299.bio: Louis-Michel van Loo was born in Toulon, France, to a family of painters. He worked in Paris and also in Spain as the court painter to King Philip V. His portraits show silk, lace and royal splendor. He died in Paris in 1771.

Q156386.bio: Henri Rousseau was born in Laval, France, and worked as a tax-and-toll collector, earning the nickname 'Le Douanier' (the customs officer). He taught himself to paint and began exhibiting in his forties. His jungle scenes, painted from visits to the Paris botanical garden, were mocked at first but later admired by Picasso and others. He died in Paris in 1910.

Q76829.bio: Alexander Ivanov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, and spent nearly 20 years in Rome working on one giant painting, 'The Appearance of Christ to the People'. He made hundreds of studies for it. He returned to Russia shortly before his death in 1858. His art deeply influenced Russian painters.

Q148475.bio: Jean-Baptiste Camille Corot was born in Paris and spent much of his life painting the French countryside and trips to Italy. His silvery, misty landscapes influenced Impressionist painters such as Monet and Pissarro. He was known as a kind and generous man. He died in Paris in 1875.

Q466639.bio: Olga Boznańska was born in Kraków, Poland, and studied in Munich and Paris, where she lived for much of her life. She became one of the most important Polish painters, with a soft, gray-toned style, and she painted many portraits. She was widely admired in Paris. She died there in 1940.

Q4027439.bio: Harald Slott-Møller was born in Denmark, near Copenhagen, and was a painter and designer. He is known for dreamy Symbolist pictures and portraits. He lived in Copenhagen and was married to the painter Agnes Slott-Møller. He died in 1937.

Q168659.bio: Franz Xaver Winterhalter was born in a small village in Germany's Black Forest and became one of the most famous painters of royalty in Europe. He worked for Queen Victoria, Napoleon III and many royal courts in Paris, London and Germany. His portraits show glittering silks and graceful poses. He died in Frankfurt in 1873.

Q213163.bio: Élisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun was born in Paris, the daughter of a painter, and became a famous portraitist at only 20. She painted Queen Marie Antoinette and fled France during the Revolution, working in Italy, Austria, Russia and England. She was one of the most successful women artists in history. She died in Paris in 1842.

Q207758.bio: Ivan Kramskoi was born in Ostrogozhsk, Russia, and worked in Saint Petersburg. He was a leader of the Wanderers, artists who rebelled against stuffy academic rules. He painted deeply felt portraits of writers, scholars and ordinary people. He also wrote and taught about art, and he inspired a generation of Russian painters.

Q319843.bio: Ford Madox Brown was born in Calais, France, to English parents and trained in Belgium before settling in London. He was a close friend of the Pre-Raphaelites, though he never formally joined them. He painted history, literature and scenes of modern working life, including the famous 'Work'. He died in London in 1893.

Q214905.bio: Thomas Eakins was born in Philadelphia and lived there nearly all his life. He studied anatomy and photography so his paintings of people, rowers and surgeons would be true to life. His honest realism upset some people, but is now praised. He taught art in Philadelphia and died there in 1916.

Q33477.bio: Eugène Delacroix was born near Paris and became the leading painter of the Romantic movement in France. He lived mostly in Paris, but a trip to Morocco in 1832 filled his sketchbooks with bright colors and scenes that inspired him for life. He believed color and emotion mattered more than perfect outlines. Later artists like Monet and Van Gogh studied his work closely.

Q353628.bio: Arkhip Kuindzhi was born in a poor family in the Mariupol area of Ukraine and trained in Saint Petersburg. He was famous for using light in his landscapes to create a nearly glowing effect, as in his moonlit nights. He lived in Saint Petersburg, where he taught and gave money to young artists. He died there in 1910.

Q127017.bio: Vasily Vereshchagin was born in Cherepovets, Russia, and traveled to Central Asia, India and the Balkans. He painted battlefields to show the true horror of war, sometimes as a war correspondent. His anti-war art shocked many viewers. He died in 1904 when a warship he was aboard struck a mine.

Q203828.bio: Gustave Moreau was born in Paris and became a leading Symbolist painter. He painted glittering scenes from myth and the Bible, with fantastic detail. He later taught at the École des Beaux-Arts, where Matisse was a student. His Paris house is now a museum.

Q194402.bio: Joshua Reynolds was born in Plympton, England, and became the first president of the Royal Academy of Arts in London. He was the most famous portrait painter of Britain in the 1700s, and he painted kings, writers, and children. He gave important lectures about art and was knighted. He died in London in 1792.

Q701669.bio: Hans Gude was born in Christiania (Oslo), Norway, and spent much of his career in Germany. He was a star of Norwegian landscape painting, depicting mountains, fjords and coasts. He taught in Düsseldorf and Berlin and trained many painters. He died in Berlin in 1903.

Q186202.bio: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was born in Venice and became the greatest Italian painter of the 1700s. He painted huge, airy ceilings full of angels, gods and clouds in churches and palaces in Italy, Germany and Spain. His light, bright colors defined the last great age of Venetian painting. He died in Madrid in 1770.

Q2339347.bio: Ivan Grohar was born in what is now Slovenia and became one of the country's best-known painters. He painted farmers and landscapes in bright, bold colors. He studied in Ljubljana and Munich. He died in Ljubljana in 1911.

Q273115.bio: Anna Bilińska-Bohdanowicz was born in Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire, to a Polish family and studied in Saint Petersburg, Munich and Paris. She lived in Warsaw and was one of the first Polish women to win international acclaim as a painter. She painted portraits and scenes in a modern style. She died young, in 1893, at age 39.

Q211356.bio: Isaac Levitan was born in Lithuania to a Jewish family and grew up in Moscow, where he studied painting. He became one of Russia's greatest landscape painters, known for his poetic scenes of rivers, forests and quiet villages. He often painted along the Volga River. He died in Moscow in 1900, at age 39.

paintings.why: Van Gogh painted this from memory while staying in a hospital in southern France, and the swirling sky seems to be alive with energy. Instead of copying what he saw, he painted how the night felt: glowing stars, a rolling wind and a sleepy village below. The bold, curling brushstrokes were revolutionary, and they showed artists they could paint emotions, not just objects. Today it is one of the most recognized paintings on Earth.

paintings.m: Department of Paintings of the Louvre
paintings.why: A woman holding the French flag charges over a barricade, with people of every background following her. Delacroix painted it after the 1830 July Revolution in Paris, and it turned a real uprising into a symbol of freedom. The drama, color and movement made it a landmark of Romantic painting. Its image of Liberty has inspired posters, stamps, and even the Statue of Liberty's story.

Van Gogh wanted to show how poor farmers really lived, so he painted a family sharing a humble meal of potatoes by lamplight. The dark, earthy colors and rough faces were deliberate: he wanted to honor honest work with hands that dug the food they ate. It was his first big masterpiece, painted long before his famous bright colors. It reminds us that great art can be about ordinary, hardworking people.

Monet painted the misty port of Le Havre at dawn, with a small orange sun and boats made of just a few quick strokes. When critics saw it in 1874, one mockingly said it was only an 'impression' — and the name Impressionism was born! The painting captures a fleeting moment of light instead of fine details. It launched a whole movement that changed how people think about painting.

Two lovers are wrapped together in a golden robe, covered in glittering patterns, kneeling on a flower-dotted meadow. Klimt used real gold leaf, which makes the painting shimmer like a jewel. He mixed flat, decorative patterns with soft, realistic faces and hands. It became the most famous work of the Vienna Secession and is loved around the world as a picture of tenderness.

The ancient Greek thinker Socrates was sentenced to drink poison, and David shows him calmly raising a finger to make one last point while friends weep around him. The clear, sculpture-like figures and calm lighting made it a model of Neoclassical painting. It is famous because it makes a big idea — standing up for your beliefs, even at great cost — feel real and powerful.

paintings.t: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
paintings.why: A lone traveler stands on a rocky peak with his back to us, gazing over a sea of mist and mountains. Friedrich wanted us to stand in his place and feel awe at nature's size and mystery. It has become the icon of Romanticism, the idea that nature and personal feelings matter deeply. We still know it because everyone has felt like that tiny wanderer at some big, quiet view.

paintings.m: Department of Paintings of the Louvre
paintings.why: In 1816 a French ship wrecked, and a handful of survivors drifted on a raft for almost two weeks. Géricault painted the moment they spot rescue far away, using huge, life-size figures and dramatic light. He even studied real survivors to get the details right. The painting was a sensation, turning a news story into a timeless picture of hope and survival against terrible odds.

According to legend, a band of Cossack warriors received an insulting demand from the Turkish sultan to surrender, and they responded with a joke-filled, rude letter. Repin shows them roaring with laughter as the scribe writes. It took him over a decade, and the laughing faces are so lively you can almost hear them. It's beloved in Ukraine and Russia for its humor and spirit.

Goya painted a woman reclining on a couch, looking directly at the viewer in a way that was bold and unusual for its time. The painting got him into trouble with the Spanish Inquisition, which only added to its fame. It is remembered for its honest, real-person feeling instead of the idealized goddesses artists usually painted. It's also famously paired with a clothed twin, La maja vestida.

Manet showed a picnic in the woods where two men in everyday suits sit with a woman who isn't dressed for the occasion — and the Paris art world was shocked. Everyone expected nudes to be goddesses from myths, not modern people at lunch. It was rejected from the official show in 1863, then displayed in the famous 'Salon of the Rejected.' It marks a turning point toward modern art.

A firing squad aims at a man in a white shirt who raises his arms, while others wait their turn in the dark. Goya painted this to remember Spanish citizens who were executed after standing up to Napoleon's army. He used a glowing lantern and a faceless line of soldiers to make the cruelty of war feel real. It's considered one of the first truly modern anti-war paintings.

paintings.t: Bal du moulin de la Galette
paintings.why: On a sunny Sunday in Montmartre, Parisians dance and chat under trees dappled with light. Renoir painted it on the spot with his friends as models, capturing the happiness of an ordinary afternoon. The flickering spots of sunlight on clothing are a hallmark of Impressionism. It's famous for making you feel as if you've joined the party, and it's one of the most valuable paintings ever sold.

A golden field under a stormy blue sky, with a path that seems to run out and crows swirling overhead. Van Gogh painted it in the final weeks of his life, and many people read deep feelings of loneliness in it. Whatever he meant, the wild brushwork and bold color are unforgettable. It's often shown as the ultimate example of how painting can carry strong emotion.

A woman reclines on a bed, looking straight at us, with a maid bringing flowers and a black cat at her feet. Manet's frank, flat style and her confident gaze scandalized visitors in 1865; some even tried to attack it. Instead of a polite myth, he painted a real modern woman who isn't shy. Today it is seen as a brave starting point of modern art.

Van Gogh painted these irises in the garden of the hospital where he was staying. The purple blooms rise and bend across a sea of green, with one lonely white flower standing out. The bold outlines were inspired by Japanese woodblock prints, which he adored. It sold for a record-setting price in 1987 and remains one of the most beloved flower paintings ever.

paintings.m: Department of Paintings of the Louvre
paintings.why: Three brothers in ancient Rome stretch out their arms to swear to fight for their city, while the women of the family weep. David's sharp lines, stage-like setting and strong sense of duty were a stunning change from the frilly paintings that came before. It helped create Neoclassicism and was admired in the years before the French Revolution as a picture of courage and sacrifice.

paintings.m: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
paintings.why: Jean-Paul Marat, a French revolutionary, lies in his bathtub after being stabbed, clutching a letter in his hand. David was his friend, and he painted it like a sacred picture, with quiet light and an empty background. It's famous because it turned a news event into a haunting memorial. The painting shows how art can shape how people remember history.
l: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium

paintings.why: A warm yellow glow from a café spills onto cobblestones beneath a deep blue night sky full of stars. Van Gogh painted this in Arles, France, and it was among the first times he painted night without using black. The contrast of orange light against blue is a joy to the eye. It still makes people want to sit down and enjoy an evening there.

A barmaid stands in front of a mirror at a busy Paris nightclub, looking sad and distant while the crowd sparkles behind her. Manet painted it near the end of his life, and the mirror reflection doesn't quite match what we'd expect, which still puzzles people. It captures the buzz of modern city life and the loneliness inside it. It's one of the great mysteries of art.

paintings.m: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens
paintings.why: A young man in a shimmering blue satin suit stands proudly against a stormy landscape. Gainsborough painted it partly to prove he could use blue as a main color — something many artists of his day believed was a mistake. It became hugely famous, and in 1922 it was shipped from England to California, drawing crowds who came to say goodbye. It's a classic of British portrait painting.
l: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

paintings.why: Van Gogh painted a late-night café in Arles with clashing reds and greens and harsh lamps glowing. He said he wanted to show a place where people could 'ruin themselves, go mad or commit a crime.' The bold colors are meant to feel uneasy. It's famous as an example of how colors alone can create a mood, and it changed the way many artists used them.

paintings.m: Department of Paintings of the Louvre
paintings.why: Napoleon, in 1804, took the crown from the Pope and placed it on his own head — and then crowned his wife Josephine, which is the moment David painted. It is enormous, about 10 meters wide, and packed with 200 life-size people. David was Napoleon's official painter, and the picture was meant to show power and glory. It's still a famous record of one of history's biggest ceremonies.

Gas lamps shimmer in long golden reflections on the river as the Big Dipper glitters overhead and a couple strolls on the shore. Van Gogh painted it outdoors at night in Arles, perhaps with candles on his hat for light. It's calmer and more peaceful than his later Starry Night, and many people consider it just as beautiful. It shows his love of the night sky.

Survivors of a shipwreck cling to a broken mast as a giant wave, the 'ninth wave' of sailors' legend, rises before them — but sunrise lights the sky with hope. Aivazovsky painted the sea so glowing and real that people felt the spray. He is Russia's most beloved painter of the ocean, and this canvas is his best-known work. It's famous for its drama and its message that hope returns with the dawn.

Goya painted this dark picture of the Roman god Saturn on the wall of his own house, never meant for anyone else to see. It's based on a myth in which a king fears his children will replace him. The wild eyes and gloomy darkness make it one of the most intense images in art. It's famous because it shows how artists can explore fear and madness — be warned, it's scary!

A twisting, wavy church stands against a deep blue sky while a woman walks on a path beside it. Van Gogh painted it in 1890, just weeks before his death, and the building almost seems alive. The strong cobalt blue sky and the curving lines give ordinary architecture a dreamlike feel. It's loved because it turns a small village church into something powerful and unforgettable.

It is exactly what it sounds like: a black square on a white background. Malevich showed it in 1915 and called it a new beginning for painting, free of any picture of the real world. He wanted art to be about pure feeling and shape. People still argue about it, and that's why it is famous: it asked 'what is art?' and changed painting forever.

Workers in a vineyard carry baskets of grapes under a blazing orange sun, with the whole field glowing red and gold. Van Gogh painted it in Arles in 1888. For a long time it was believed to be the only painting he sold during his life, though that is now thought to be uncertain. It remains famous for its heat and bright, joyful colors.

This is the actual house in Arles, France, where Van Gogh lived and hoped to start a community of artists. He painted it with a bright blue sky and a sunny, buttery yellow — his color for happiness. Fellow painter Paul Gauguin stayed there, but the friendship went badly. It's loved as a cheerful portrait of a hopeful dream, and as a window into his life.

Eleven men, bent over and tied to ropes, drag a heavy boat up a river in the burning sun. Repin saw this hard labor himself, and he painted each man as a real person with his own story. It shocked Russian viewers who had rarely seen working people shown with such respect. It's celebrated as a masterpiece of Russian realism and a call for compassion.

paintings.t: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
paintings.why: Parisians relax by a river on a sunny Sunday — but the whole picture is made of tiny dots of pure color! Seurat spent two years on it, studying the science of how our eyes mix colors. Standing back, the dots blend into glowing light. This technique, called pointillism, was brand new. It's famous for being both a quiet picnic and a daring experiment.

A fashionable Viennese lady sits in a glimmering swirl of gold, patterns and eyes, with only her face and hands painted realistically. Klimt covered the canvas in gold leaf, like a Byzantine mosaic. During World War II the painting was taken from its owners, and decades later her family won it back in a famous legal case. Its story is as dramatic as its sparkle.

A young woman in a frothy pink dress swings high in a leafy garden while a man hides in the bushes and another gives her a push. Fragonard painted it for a rich French nobleman, and the whole thing is playful, fluffy and fun. Her shoe is flying off into the air! It's the best-known painting of the Rococo style, which celebrated lightness and delight.

paintings.m: Department of Paintings of the Louvre
paintings.why: A woman reclines on a couch with her back to us, looking over her shoulder. Ingres stretched her body longer than is natural, adding extra vertebrae on purpose to create a graceful curve. Critics at the time found it strange, but today it's admired for its elegant lines and silky textures. It's an important example of how artists sometimes break reality for beauty.

Courbet painted a funeral in his small hometown on a canvas as big as a history painting. The mourners are ordinary villagers, shown just as they were, without glamor. In 1850 this was shocking, since big canvases were reserved for kings and heroes. It is famous as a landmark of Realism, the idea that everyday people deserve to be painted as important.

A young woman floats in a river among flowers, singing as she drifts, based on a scene from Shakespeare's Hamlet. Millais painted every leaf and petal with incredible detail, spending months outdoors beside a river. The model, Elizabeth Siddal, lay in a bathtub filled with water for hours. It's one of the most beloved works of the Pre-Raphaelites, who loved nature and storytelling.

paintings.t: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
paintings.why: Gauguin painted this huge canvas in Tahiti as a kind of life story, from a baby on the right to an old woman on the left. The title asks three of life's biggest questions. He considered it his masterpiece and said he painted it before planning to end his life, though he lived on. It's famous for its dreamy colors and for asking questions everyone wonders about.

The Roman goddess Venus rises from the sea on a shell, surrounded by cherubs and carried to shore on the wind. Bouguereau painted her with a smooth, porcelain finish popular in the French Salon. It was a huge hit when new and made him one of the most famous painters in the world. It's a showpiece of academic painting.

paintings.t: Ivan the Terrible and his son Ivan on November 16, 1581
paintings.why: A Russian tsar cradles his own son, whom he has just struck in a fit of rage, and stares in horror at what he's done. Repin painted the terror and regret on his face so well that it shocked viewers; one even slashed the canvas in 1913 and had to be repaired. It's famous for its raw emotion and for how it shows that power can lead to tragedy.

Women in Breton costumes kneel around a bright yellow crucifix in a golden autumn field. Gauguin was inspired by a wooden carving in a village chapel in Brittany, France. He used flat, bold colors and dark outlines instead of realistic shading. It's a landmark of Synthetism, a style that favored feeling and symbol over copying the world.

paintings.m: Musée des Beaux-Arts de la ville de Paris
paintings.why: Two women rest in each other's arms on a rumpled bed, caught in a quiet moment. Courbet was a Realist, who wanted to paint life honestly, and the painting was considered scandalous when it was made. Today, it's admired for its soft light and gentle skin tones. It remains an important example of how artists began exploring private moments.

Officially titled 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1', this portrait shows Whistler's mother sitting quietly in profile, with a plain wall and a framed print behind her. Whistler cared about shapes and colors, like musical notes, more than about the story. It became a symbol of motherhood and has been parodied for over a century. It's even been called America's most famous painting.

Two women sit on the ground in Tahiti in bright colorful clothes, one gazing out with a serious look. Gauguin moved to the South Pacific hoping to find a simpler world, and his bold colors and flat shapes helped inspire modern art. The title is a question put to a woman by her neighbors. In 2015 it was reported to have sold for around $300 million, among the highest prices ever.

A blazing orange sunset glows over a wild hillside of twisted trees near Arles. For many years, the painting sat forgotten in an attic and was believed to be fake — until 2013, when experts confirmed it as a real Van Gogh. It was a big news story! It's special because it reveals a rare, undiscovered landscape by one of history's most loved artists.

Four bear cubs play on a fallen tree in a misty pine forest at dawn. Shishkin painted the trees and Savitsky added the bears, though the museum collector later erased Savitsky's name from the signature! The golden light filtering through the fog makes you feel the cool morning air. It is one of the best-loved paintings in Russia, famous even from candy wrappers.

paintings.t: Charles IV of Spain and His Family
paintings.why: Goya painted the royal family of Spain standing in a stiff row, dressed in their grandest clothes. But look closer: the faces look ordinary, even a bit unflattering, and Goya himself is peeking from the back left, just as Velázquez did in 'Las Meninas'. He painted the royals with surprising honesty. It's admired for its sparkling fabrics and for its clever, daring truthfulness.

paintings.m: Department of Paintings of the Louvre
paintings.why: An ancient king lounges on a huge bed, calmly watching his palace be destroyed in a whirlwind of red, gold and chaos. Delacroix based it on a poem by Lord Byron. Critics in 1827 thought it was messy and over the top. But its explosion of color and action thrilled other artists, and it became a landmark of the Romantic movement.

Courbet shows himself painting a landscape in the center of a huge room, surrounded by friends, models, and the poor on the other side. He called it a 'real allegory' of his life as an artist. The huge scale, usually reserved for history paintings, was a bold statement. It's famous for declaring that a painter's own world is worth painting.

Friends laugh, flirt and share wine on a sunny balcony beside the Seine river. Renoir painted his real friends, and the woman at left holding a little dog became his future wife. Light dances over the tablecloth, the fruit, and everyone's straw hats. It's one of the happiest paintings ever made and is why people still smile when they see it.

A woman and a man sit side by side at a Paris café, yet each seems lost in their own lonely thoughts. Degas placed them off-center and tilted the tables, as if a camera snapped the scene by accident. Viewers in 1876 were not used to such honest, unglamorous pictures. It remains famous for showing the quiet sadness that can exist inside a busy city.

A farm cart splashes across a shallow stream in front of a cottage, beneath a huge sky of drifting clouds. Constable painted the scene near his boyhood home in Suffolk, England, and it's full of real countryside. When it was shown in Paris in 1824, French artists were amazed by its fresh, natural look. It has become one of the most beloved images of the English countryside.

An old man sits in a chair with his head buried in his fists, overwhelmed by sorrow. Van Gogh painted it in 1890 from an earlier drawing, near the end of his life, and said he wanted to show deep feelings. The thick, wavy brushstrokes and strong blue make the sadness easy to see. It's powerful because it shows emotion anyone can understand.

A girl in a glowing yellow dress leans on a plump pillow, absorbed in her book. Fragonard painted her with quick, feathery brushwork, almost like he was sketching in paint. It celebrates the quiet pleasure of reading, which still feels familiar today. It's one of the most charming pictures in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
